name: Clinical care
description: Bedside care for exercises and unfolding case studies: vital signs and early warning scores, lab results with reference ranges, medication administration records, SBAR handoffs, triage tags, staffing grids, isolation boards and evacuation lists. One library of synthetic patients serves tabletop play (a unit surge, an evacuation, an outbreak, a downtime shift) and case studies in which a patient's story unfolds in stages and the learner decides at each stage. Exercise content, never clinical guidance.

advisorRoles.name: Clinical educator
advisorRoles.description: Checks that patient data, nursing actions and the sequence of care are plausible and coherent.

advisorRoles.name: Rapid response team lead
advisorRoles.description: Answers rapid response calls and decides on transfer to a higher level of care.

advisorRoles.name: Physician advisor
advisorRoles.description: Plays the covering provider: orders, call-backs and the questions a provider asks a nurse.

advisorRoles.name: Infection preventionist
advisorRoles.description: Advises on precautions, cohorting and outbreak notification.

advisorRoles.name: Simulation facilitator
advisorRoles.description: Runs the prebrief and the structured debrief of a case study or tabletop.

glossary.definition: The NCSBN model of six cognitive operations behind nursing judgment: recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action and evaluate outcomes. Case study prompts name the step they test.
One patient's story revealed in stages; at each stage the learner sees new data and answers prompts, and the next stage depends on the choices.

Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation: a structured way to hand over concerns by phone or in person. A good SBAR states the patient, the problem now, the relevant history, the nurse's assessment of severity and a clear request. Read-back confirms the receiver heard it.
A structured handoff mnemonic (Introduction, Patient, Assessment, Situation, Safety concerns, the Background, Actions, Timing, Ownership, Next).

A composite of vital sign parameters turned into a total that triggers an escalation. The parameters, bands, triggers and recommended responses are a configuration; a named published score is used only with its source cited.
A team called to a patient who is deteriorating but not in arrest, to assess at the bedside and decide on a higher level of care.
Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment: sorts casualties by ability to walk, respirations, perfusion and mental status into minor, delayed, immediate and expectant or deceased.
Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment and/or Transport: a mass casualty triage approach that adds lifesaving interventions and a sort by response to commands.
Assigning a lower or higher category than the patient's findings warrant.
A lab result so far outside the normal range that the laboratory must call a provider or nurse at once; the time of the call and read-back are documented.
Medication administration record: scheduled, given, held, refused and late doses for a patient.
Right patient, drug, dose, route and time, with further rights added in many programs.
The number of patients assigned to one nurse; the safe number depends on acuity, unit type and state law.
How sick a patient is and how much nursing care they need.
Grouping patients with the same infection in one area with dedicated staff.
Transmission-based isolation measures added to standard precautions according to how an organism spreads.
Moving patients to another floor (vertical) or behind a fire door on the same floor (horizontal).
A period when the electronic record or related systems are unavailable and care is documented on paper.

The briefing before a simulation (objectives, ground rules, confidentiality, psychological safety, orientation) and the structured conversation afterward that reflects on what happened. Both are planned parts of the simulation.
Telling a patient or family about a harm event promptly and plainly, with a named lead, what is known, what is not and what happens next.
A short debrief immediately after an exercise.

productConventions: Every patient is synthetic and labeled as exercise content; names are fictional and never those of real people.

A vital-signs entry has a date and time, heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation (with room air or the flow of oxygen), temperature (with units) and level of consciousness.

A lab result states the test, the value, the units, the reference range and a flag (H, L, or critical) that agrees with the range shown; a critical value records who was called, when, and the read-back.
An early warning score is shown as the parameters with their points, the total, the trigger band and the recommended response. The arithmetic must add up.
An SBAR has all four elements; when an element is deliberately missing, the product shows the gap rather than hiding it.
A triage tag shows the category, the findings that produced it (breathing, perfusion, mental status, ability to walk) and the time; the category agrees with the findings under the stated method.
A medication line has drug, dose, units, route, frequency and the scheduled time; given doses record the time and the nurse's initials; held or late doses record the reason.
A staffing grid shows needed, scheduled, called in and agency counts per shift and the resulting nurse-to-patient ratio; the numbers add up.
An evacuation list has one row per patient with bed, name, acuity and dependency (ventilator, infusion, bariatric, infant), the equipment that goes with the patient, the destination and the time out.
Times use the 24-hour clock; weights and doses use the metric system; temperatures state Celsius or Fahrenheit.
A case study stage shows only data the learner would have at that point; it never reveals the next stage's results.

Exercise evaluation guides for nursing exercises name critical tasks a nurse can be observed doing. Mass Care Services: assign beds, nurses and supplies to arriving patients and keep ratios within the plan. Public Health, Healthcare and EMS: triage and reassess casualties, isolate and cohort infectious patients, notify public health.

More critical tasks for nursing evaluation guides. Operational Coordination: escalate a staffing shortage to the house supervisor with a number and a request. Operational Communications: give a structured SBAR report with read-back, and notify the provider of a critical result. Situational Assessment: reassess vital signs and the early warning score at the stated interval and keep the census and patient tracking current.
realismRules: Vital signs, labs and findings follow one coherent physiologic story; a patient in septic shock does not have a normal lactate and a normal blood pressure unless the case says why.
Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature stay within human ranges and change gradually over time unless an event explains a jump.

Doses and routes are plausible for the named drug and patient; when unsure, name the drug and a typical adult dose range from a standard reference and flag it for review; never invent an implausible dose.
A nurse does not diagnose or prescribe; nursing actions are assessment, monitoring, nursing interventions within standing orders, escalation and documentation, and requests for orders.
Rapid response is called for deterioration, not arrest; a code is called for arrest. Do not mix them.
Hand hygiene for C. difficile uses soap and water; contact precautions with a gown and gloves apply. Alcohol hand rub does not kill the spores.
A handoff carries allergies, code status, isolation status, lines and drains, and pending results; a handoff missing these is the kind of gap a case study may deliberately show.
Staff ratios and patient flow numbers must add up across injects: beds, census, arrivals, discharges and nurses on duty.
A lab flag matches the reference range printed beside it; units and ranges match the test.

Triage categories follow the findings under START or SALT: a casualty who walks is minor; one who breathes only after repositioning, or has absent radial pulse, or cannot follow commands is immediate under START. Expectant is a resource decision, stated as such.
Content involving patient death, violence, or harm to children carries a content notice and an opt-out for learners.
No real patient data, real people or real hospitals; fictional teaching hospitals and units only. Real city names and public agencies are permitted.
Do not reproduce NCLEX items or any licensed exam content; write original prompts.
The score and recommendation text on a chart cite their source; a named published score is used only when its terms are confirmed.
